title: Anisotropic magnon spin transport in CrPS$_4$
authors: Krishnaraajan Sundararajan, Muhammad Zohaib, Yulia Kreminska, Sytze H. Tirion, Bart J. van Wees
abstract: Crystal anisotropy provides a powerful route for realizing direction-dependent transport in solid-state systems. While its influence on electronic transport is well established, the role of anisotropy in magnon spin transport in van der Waals magnets is largely unexplored. Here, in a nonlocal geometry, utilizing the monoclinic van der Waals antiferromagnet CrPS$_4$, we observe pronounced anisotropy in both electrically and in thermally excited magnon spin transport. Electrically generated magnons exhibit a magnon spin conductivity at least 2.2 times larger and a spin diffusion length at least 2.7 times longer for transport along the crystallographic-b axis compared to the crystallographic-a axis, where $λ_m^{a} \sim$ 211 nm and $λ_m^{b} \geq$ 575 nm. In comparison, at 8T, we find the nonlocal second-harmonic resistance associated with thermally excited magnons to be $\sim$7 times larger along the crystallographic-b axis at 25K. We further show that a magnon spin diffusion length cannot be reliably extracted from the nonlocal second-harmonic resistance, owing to the extended temperature profile within CrPS$_4$. Likewise, we show that the anisotropy in the spin Seebeck coefficients cannot be reliably estimated from the thermally excited magnon spin transport alone, as it is intertwined with the anisotropic heat conductivity of CrPS$_4$. Utilizing the electrically generated magnon spin transport, we demonstrate that intrinsic crystalline anisotropy serves as an effective control parameter for tuning magnon spin transport, opening new avenues for magnonic device engineering.
summary: This work experimentally demonstrates that crystal anisotropy strongly controls magnon spin transport in $	ext{CrPS}_4$. By measuring nonlocal magnetotransport signals, the authors quantify direction-dependent properties like conductivity and diffusion length. The findings establish intrinsic crystalline structure as a powerful tool for designing next-generation magnonic devices.
main_problem: The study investigates how crystal anisotropy dictates the direction-dependent transport properties of magnon spin currents in van der Waals magnets.
main_result: Pronounced anisotropic magnon spin conductivity and diffusion lengths were observed when using electrically generated magnons, confirming that intrinsic crystalline anisotropy is a key control parameter for magnonic device engineering.
method: The research employs nonlocal magnetotransport measurements (both first- and second-harmonic resistance) on patterned Platinum strips deposited on the $	ext{CrPS}_4$ antiferromagnet.
model_or_system: The physical system is the monoclinic van der Waals antiferromagnet $	ext{CrPS}_4$. The analysis utilizes magnon spin diffusion models incorporating anisotropic exchange couplings ($J_1, J_2, J_3$) and measures transport along crystallographic $a$ and $b$ axes.
key_observables: Magnon spin conductivity ($\sigma_m$), magnon spin diffusion length ($\lambda_m$), nonlocal first-harmonic resistance ($R_{NL}^{1\omega}$), and nonlocal second-harmonic resistance ($R_{NL}^{2\omega}$).
important_parameters: Temperature (e.g., 25 K, 15 K), magnetic field strength (up to 8 T), and crystallographic direction ($\hat{a}$ vs $\hat{b}$).
main_assumptions: Electrically generated magnon transport is preferred over thermal excitation for isolating intrinsic anisotropy effects; extracting $\lambda_m$ from thermal measurements is complicated by temperature gradients.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the crystal structure and device geometry, showing how Pt electrodes are patterned along $a$ and $b$ axes. Results plot nonlocal resistances versus magnetic field or separation distance to quantify directional differences.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical framework for anisotropic magnon diffusion, details the experimental setup using nonlocal magnetotransport measurements on $	ext{CrPS}_4$, presents quantitative comparisons between electrical and thermal excitation regimes, and concludes by emphasizing anisotropy control.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter magnetism, the study of spin transport dynamics and engineered directional responses in crystalline materials provides a solid experimental platform for understanding energy/momentum channeling effects relevant to quantum devices.
